title: The Words of Agur: Humble Wisdom and Numbered Wonders
summary: An otherwise unknown sage named Agur confesses his weariness and ignorance before God, asks who has ascended to heaven, and affirms that every word of God is flawless. He prays for neither poverty nor riches, then offers a series of observations, many arranged in numbered lists, on arrogant generations, insatiable things, wonders he cannot understand, things that upset the social order, small but wise creatures, and stately walkers.
story: After the long collections of Solomon's proverbs, the book of Proverbs turns in its last two chapters to two otherwise unknown voices, Agur and King Lemuel. Chapter 30 is Agur's, and it strikes a different tone from much of the book. Where earlier chapters speak with the confidence of a father teaching his son, Agur begins by confessing how little he knows. Placed near the book's end, his humility is a fitting counterweight: the wisdom Proverbs has offered is real, but it rests finally on God's word, not on human mastery.
historical:
Agur son of Jakeh appears nowhere else in Scripture, and nothing certain is known about him. The word translated burden in verse 1 (massa) can mean an oracle or prophetic utterance, but it is also the name of an Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14). Some scholars therefore think Agur came from Massa, which would make him a non-Israelite sage, much like Job, whose home in Uz lay outside Israel. Others take massa as a description of his words as a weighty pronouncement. The same word appears in 31:1 for Lemuel.

The first verse is one of the hardest in the book to translate. Older translations read it as names: the man spoke to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal. Many modern translations, including the Berean Standard Bible, divide and vocalize the Hebrew consonants differently, producing Agur's opening cry: “I am weary, O God, and worn out.” Both readings are possible from the Hebrew letters, and translators disagree.
cultural:
The numerical saying, which gives a number and then that number plus one (three things, four things), was a common device in ancient Near Eastern wisdom. It appears in Ugaritic texts, in Amos 1 and 2, and elsewhere in Proverbs (6:16-19). The pattern invites the listener to think about what the items have in common, and the last item usually carries the emphasis.

The animals of verses 24 to 31 were familiar to Agur's hearers. The rock badger (the hyrax) is a small animal that lives among rocks in the Judean wilderness and the Negev. Locusts moved in huge swarms that could strip a land bare, so their advance without a king was both a wonder and a terror. The lizard, easily caught, still managed to live in royal palaces. The fate of the mocking eye in verse 17, plucked out by ravens, reflects the ancient horror of dying without burial, left exposed in an open valley.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 9 are a confession and prayer in the first person. Agur's rhetorical questions in verse 4 recall God's questions to Job from the whirlwind (Job 38 to 41), which likewise humble human understanding before the Creator. Verses 5 and 6 draw on earlier Scripture: verse 5 closely resembles Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31, and verse 6 echoes Deuteronomy 4:2, which forbids adding to God's commands. Verses 10 to 33 are observations, most of them in numbered lists. Verses 11 to 14 form a sequence of four lines each beginning with the word generation, and the chapter closes with a warning to put your hand over your mouth, a gesture of silence.

outline.t: A prayer for neither poverty nor riches
Insatiable things and the eye that mocks
Four things that make the earth tremble
Four stately walkers, and a call to silence

doctrines.note: After confessing he cannot reach wisdom by his own effort, Agur turns to God's word: “Every word of God is flawless.” Human wisdom has limits, but God's revealed word is tested and true, and it must not be added to.

The chapter draws lessons from the world God made: the eagle, the snake, the ant, the rock badger, the locust, the lizard, the lion. Creation itself is a place to learn wisdom, a theme that runs through Proverbs.

Agur's prayer (verses 7 to 9) asks for integrity and for enough, not too much and not too little, so that he will neither forget God in plenty nor dishonor him in want. It is one of the Old Testament's most searching prayers about money.

words.note: Massa, a burden, an oracle, or possibly a place name. The word is used by the prophets for weighty pronouncements from God. In verse 1 it may describe Agur's words as an oracle or identify his homeland as Massa, an Arabian people. Translators are divided.

Tsaraph, to refine or test by fire, as a metalworker purifies silver. Verse 5 says every word of God is refined, flawless, like metal that has been smelted and has no impurity left. The image speaks of reliability proven by testing.

Chasah, to take refuge. God is a shield to those who take refuge in him. The verb is common in the Psalms and pictures fleeing to a shelter. Agur pairs the reliability of God's word with the safety of trusting God himself.

Qadosh, holy. Agur says he has no knowledge of the Holy One (verse 3), a title for God that stresses his otherness and moral purity. The plural form used here likely expresses majesty. Agur's humility begins with recognizing how far God is above him.

christ: Agur's question in verse 4, who has ascended to heaven and come down, and what is his name and the name of his Son, has drawn much reflection. In context, the questions stress that no human has done these things and that only God has. Jewish interpreters have often understood the son as Israel, whom God calls his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). Christian readers have heard an echo that the New Testament answers: Jesus says in John 3:13 that no one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man. The New Testament doesn't quote this verse directly, and Agur was not describing the Trinity, but the question he asks, who can bridge heaven and earth, is one the gospel claims Christ answers. His prayer for the bread that is his portion is also close in spirit to the request for daily bread in the prayer Jesus taught (Matthew 6:11), a thematic link rather than a prediction.

hard.q: Who is the Son in verse 4, and is this a prophecy of Christ?
hard.a: Verse 4 asks a string of questions whose expected answer is that no human has done these things, only God: gathering the wind, binding up the waters, establishing the ends of the earth. The final question, what is his name and the name of his Son, is harder. Some interpreters, especially in Jewish tradition, understand the son as Israel, since God calls Israel his son in Exodus 4:22 and elsewhere. Others think the question is an ironic challenge, like God's questions to Job (compare Job 38:4-5): no human can name the one who does these things or claim to know his household, and the closing “surely you know” exposes the pretension of anyone who claims otherwise. Many Christian interpreters have read the verse as a glimpse of the Son who shares God's work of creation, in light of the New Testament's teaching that all things were made through Christ. The verse itself does not explain the son, and the most careful readings let it remain an open question that the rest of Scripture takes up.

questions: Agur begins by confessing his ignorance. How does admitting what you don't know make space for wisdom?
Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches. What would it mean for you to pray for enough, and what do you fear about having too much or too little?
Which of the small but wise creatures in verses 24 to 28 has a lesson you need right now?
